thread.title: Is Commercial Banking Catching Up On Its Use Of Information Technology?

author: John M. Mason
title: Is Commercial Banking Catching Up On Its Use Of Information Technology?
text:
Commercial banking has been notoriously lagging in its adoption of the latest information technology developments. The only industry that seemed to be even further behind in its adaption of cutting-edge approaches in this space has been the health care industry.
How great is it to known in this field as being just ahead of health care?
Over the past couple of years I have reported on conferences held at places like MIT that have focused upon FinTech and the introduction of current information technology practices into the commercial banking industry and a common theme heard at these meetings has been how far behind the commercial banking system seems to be in terms of catching up with other industries and other countries.
Leaders in the banking industry were not stepping out too far and were certainly not speaking a lot about what was going on.
Well, progress seems to be making some headway.
Earlier this month JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM ) announced some of the "new" things it was doing to change the environment, and this included hiring major academic talent in the area of machine learning. Spending on technology in 2018 at JPMorgan will total about $10.8 billion.
Now, “ Citigroup; Big Bank, Big Spender on Tech ” is jumping into the picture.
“Citigroup (NYSE: C ) spent $8 billion on technology in 2017, easily more than was invested by venture capital across all U.S. financial technology startups last year.”
“Chief Executive Michael Corbat, speaking to investors at a conference Wednesday, said that about 20% of the bank’s expenses go to technology, which translates roughly into a more than $8 billion annual tech budget based on last year’s expenses.”
New York Times reporter Telis Demos writes in this article “The gap highlights how furiously banks are spending to keep themselves ahead of potential upstart competitors.”
Demos adds, “The big figures also give a sense of how much banks are betting that new technology, ranging from robotic process automation to open-ledger blockchain systems, can help slash costs over the longer term.”
This is all good news as far as the banking industry is concerned, but this last statement raises another issue that is concerning.
The commercial banks are responding the way “legacy” industries usually respond. We are, they say, bumping up spending on technology, so as to reduce costs and make existing product lines more competitive and, hence, more capable of keeping us in business as we know it.
The Catch-22 here is that they are attempting to improve the business as they know it.
The problem with this is that the whole world is going through a transformation right now, and the indications are that if managements “keep the business as they know it” they are going to be history.
I have just been writing about the changes that are taking place in major corporations…the really successful ones. What we are seeing is that the new “modern” technology requires more than just introducing new modern technology into the organization.
As I try and explain in “ Apple: the Epitome of Where the Modern Corporation is Going" and “ Apple: Where the Modern Corporation is Going--II ,” the new corporation is not just specifically about what is being produced. The modern corporation is all about networks and how things fit together and intellectual property, and…most of all…about information.
Even more crucial to banks should be the realization that finance is nothing more than information, zeros and ones. Commercial banks… and other financial institutions…need to accept the reality of this fact and identify what this really means for their future.
But, it’s not just the FinTech’s that are the big worry. It seems as if most of the rest of the world is focusing upon the “payments” mechanism and here you get into what Apple is doing, what Amazon is doing, what the Chinese are doing , and so forth.
This seems as if they are saying, focus upon payments, all the rest of finance is in the network.
The most progressive non-financial organizations are structuring their existence around networks, not products and services.
The latest news is that even Microsoft is moving structurally into this space.
“Five years ago, Microsoft looked at risk of missing the next big architectural shifts in computing. Its shares had been rangebound for more than a dozen years, as other tech companies took the lead in mobile and cloud computing.”
“A low point: after losing the smartphone software market to Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) and Google (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) (NASDAQ: GOOG ), former chief executive Steve Ballmer gambled on an acquisition of Nokia’s (NYSE: NOK ) handset business to catch up. The deal, universally hated on Wall Street, was a failure; Mr Ballmer stepped down in 2014.”
“The change since then has been startling. With cloud services delivering a jolt of growth, Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT ) is expected to post its fastest revenue expansion for a decade when its financial year ends next month. Its shares are up three-fold.”
“That has won an army of new Wall Street supporters for Mr. Ballmer’s successor, Satya Nadella, who had made his mark as Microsoft’s cloud boss.”
Mr. Ballmer had been locked into the past and this cost him. Mr. Nadella has moved Microsoft into the evolving view of what the corporation will look like in the future.
Commercial bankers cannot just ‘buy” more technology and reduce costs. If the “new” technology is not a part of a “new” structural framework of banking organizations built around networks and intellectual capital then the more and more of these institutions will just become legacy. The Chinese, if no one else, will see to that!
Bank leaders cannot be very smug about what they are doing thinking that big pending will keep them in the game. The new technology represents a new world, and this new world requires something more than just adding gimmicks to their products with the hope that such actions is all they need to do.
